## The idea

Play the white notes from D to D over a sustained D. The collection is identical
to C major, yet C no longer sounds like home. The drone changes every note's
role. The raised sixth, B, gives the line a brightness that D natural minor would
lose.

A *mode* is a scale pattern heard around a particular tonic. Rotating the major
step formula creates seven modes: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian,
Aeolian, and Locrian. Rotation alone is mathematically correct and musically
insufficient. Without a stable root, your ear may keep reinterpreting the notes
as their parent major scale. The drone fixes the address space.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

define :build_scale do |root, steps|
  notes = [root]
  steps.each { |step| notes << notes[-1] + step }
  notes
end

define :play_mode do |root, steps|
  notes = build_scale(root, steps)
  in_thread do
    synth :dark_ambience, note: root - 12, sustain: 7.5,
      release: 0.5, amp: 0.45
  end
  (notes + notes[1..-2].reverse).each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.32
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

major_steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1]
names = [:ionian, :dorian, :phrygian, :lydian,
         :mixolydian, :aeolian, :locrian]

names.each_with_index do |name, index|
  puts name
  play_mode(note(:d4), major_steps.rotate(index))
  sleep 1
end
```

Every pass starts and ends on D, so the changed step pattern has to reveal
itself against one reference. Lydian's raised fourth produces a conspicuous
lift. Phrygian's lowered second crowds the tonic. Mixolydian sounds major until
its lowered seventh removes the leading-tone pull.

## Change one thing

1. Restrict the loop to Ionian, Dorian, and Mixolydian. These separate into
   major, minor-with-raised-sixth, and major-with-lowered-seventh. Hear the
   characteristic degree before adding the remaining modes.
2. Remove the drone thread. The pitch lists remain accurate, but the tonal
   centre becomes less secure. Notice which modes collapse most readily into a
   nearby major scale.
3. Replace `:d4` with `:fs3`. The modes transpose while their interval patterns
   remain unchanged. Keep the drone an octave below the new root.

## Why it works

Array rotation preserves the multiset of steps and changes their order. Because
the values still sum to twelve, each mode closes at the octave. The semitone
positions move relative to the root, altering which degrees feel tense or
settled.

It helps to compare each mode with major or natural minor. Ionian is major.
Dorian resembles natural minor with a raised sixth. Phrygian has a lowered
second. Lydian resembles major with a raised fourth. Mixolydian lowers major's
seventh. Aeolian is natural minor. Locrian lowers the second and fifth of natural
minor, leaving its tonic chord unstable.

The characteristic degree is a diagnostic rather than a complete definition.
A melody that never touches Dorian's sixth gives your ear little evidence. The
ascending and descending program visits every degree, so the comparison is
fair. Later melodies can emphasise the diagnostic note with duration, accent,
or repetition.

The common root is the experimental control. If every mode began on the white
key associated with its rotation, pitch height and tonic would change together.
Starting all seven on D forces the interval pattern to carry the contrast. It
also avoids the mistaken claim that Dorian belongs only to D or Mixolydian only
to G. Any mode can begin on any pitch once its steps are applied from that root.

## Take it further

Build an ear drill containing Ionian, Dorian, and Mixolydian. Start with
`use_random_seed 42`, choose one mode, play its drone and a six-note phrase that
includes its characteristic degree, wait four beats, then print and play the
answer. Run ten trials. Store the modes as data and keep the phrase rhythm
identical so mode is the changing variable.
